title: MemMux: Runtime Verification and Honest Resource Attribution for Fleets of Parallel Coding Agents
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:MemMux: Runtime Verification and Honest Resource Attribution for Fleets of Parallel Coding Agents
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Developers increasingly run a fleet of coding agents side by side on one workstation. The tools they reach for, terminal multiplexers like tmux and a new generation of agent managers, were built to arrange windows, not to govern memory. When ten agents each spawn language servers, test runners, and browsers, no standard tool can say how much memory belongs to which agent, confirm that a terminated agent's descendants are gone, notice a child that has escaped its agent, or keep the machine off the swap cliff when an OOM kill would silently discard uncommitted work. We treat these as runtime-verification problems: an agent-hosting substrate should continuously emit observable signals an operator or auditor can check while agents run. We present MemMux, a local runtime that turns resource governance into checkable signals (per-agent attribution, complete reclamation, escaped-process visibility, bounded footprint under overcommit, and monitoring overhead), with a claims-disciplined benchmark against tmux, a purpose-built agent multiplexer, and a raw-process baseline on identical workloads. Under a binding memory budget on a Linux host, MemMux keeps the fleet under budget (7.5 GiB) with zero swap by admitting a subset and reclaiming under pressure, while the ungoverned tools run every agent, pin the machine at its RAM ceiling (2x over budget), and spill about 2 GiB into swap. MemMux reclaims 100% of a terminated agent's process subtree where the raw baseline strands half of it, and it alone surfaces escaped children (10 of 10 detected). We report the cost: the 1 Hz attribution scan runs near 0.6% CPU at one agent but 2.7% at ten, above our 2% target. Running the harness on real Claude Code sessions shows 100% attribution and low overhead carry over to live agent trees. We release the engine, benchmark, and a one-command reproducer.

report.summary: MemMux is a local runtime that gives fleets of parallel coding agents verifiable per-agent memory attribution, complete process reclamation, and bounded footprint, avoiding swap and silent OOM data loss.
report.background: Developers increasingly run many coding agents side by side on a single workstation, and each agent spawns heavyweight children such as language servers, test runners, and browsers. The tools used to manage these fleets — terminal multiplexers like tmux and early agent managers — were designed to arrange windows, not to govern memory. As a result, operators cannot tell how much memory belongs to which agent, whether a terminated agent's descendants are truly gone, or whether a child process has escaped its parent. When the machine hits its RAM ceiling, an OOM kill can silently discard uncommitted work, and swap thrashing degrades every agent at once. MemMux reframes resource governance as a runtime-verification problem, demanding continuously observable signals that an operator or auditor can check while agents run.
key_points: The paper treats agent resource governance as runtime verification, defining five checkable signals: per-agent memory attribution, complete reclamation of terminated subtrees, visibility of escaped processes, bounded footprint under overcommit, and monitoring overhead. The goal is not just better scheduling but evidence an operator can continuously verify during execution.

Under a binding 7.5 GiB memory budget on Linux, MemMux keeps the agent fleet under budget with zero swap by admitting a subset of agents and reclaiming memory under pressure. Ungoverned tools, including tmux, ran every agent, pinned the machine at twice the budget, and spilled roughly 2 GiB into swap.

Reclamation is dramatically more complete: MemMux reclaims 100% of a terminated agent's process subtree, whereas the raw-process baseline strands about half of it. This matters because orphaned language servers and browsers quietly consume memory and can keep ports or files locked long after an agent is stopped.

Escaped-process detection is unique to MemMux in the benchmark: it surfaced 10 of 10 escaped children, while the other approaches detected none. The 1 Hz attribution scan costs near 0.6% CPU with one agent and 2.7% with ten, above the authors' 2% target, an honest reported limitation.

Validation on real Claude Code sessions showed 100% attribution and low overhead carrying over to live agent trees, not just synthetic workloads. The authors release the engine, the benchmark, and a one-command reproducer, and they describe the work as a claims-disciplined comparison against tmux, a purpose-built agent multiplexer, and a raw-process baseline.
report.impact: For the AI industry, MemMux signals that agent fleets are becoming a first-class workload requiring governed, auditable infrastructure rather than ad hoc window management. Developers gain visibility into which agent owns which memory, confidence that stopped agents leave no orphans, and protection against OOM kills destroying uncommitted work. Agent-manager and terminal-multiplexer vendors now have a clear feature bar: per-agent attribution, subtree reclamation, and escape detection. Regular users running several agents locally get more predictable machines, though the 2.7% CPU overhead at ten agents shows governance is not free. The benchmark discipline could become a template for evaluating agent infrastructure, and the escaped-child finding raises audit and accountability questions for enterprise deployments.
report.tools: Follow the MemMux paper's released engine, benchmark, and one-command reproducer. Related tools worth watching: tmux and purpose-built agent multiplexers such as Claude Squad or Crystal; Linux cgroups v2 and systemd slices for memory budgets; eBPF or psutil-based process monitoring for subtree and escape tracking; and container isolation via Docker or Podman for stronger per-agent boundaries. Claude Code sessions are the paper's live validation target.
